issues.legal_issue: A temple dedicated for the benefit of a section of the Hindu community falls within the scope of a public-temple-entry law where its private status was not pleaded and coverage under the amended definition was admitted.
material_facts: The temple was dedicated for the benefit of a particular Hindu community.
The plaintiffs did not plead that the temple was private, despite the amended definition encompassing temples dedicated for the benefit of a section of the Hindu community.
The plaintiffs admitted that the temple fell within the amended definition.
issues.conclusion: The temple was a public temple within the operation of the Act. The Court declined to entertain the contention that it was private because that contention had not been pleaded.
issues.legal_principle: A party must plead a material factual contention so the opposing party can controvert it and adduce evidence. A court should not use evidence introduced on an issue that was tried to decide a different issue that was not pleaded. Under section 2(2), as amended, a temple dedicated for the benefit of a section of the Hindu community is covered.

rule.if: temple_entry_scope_case and private_status_not_pleaded and temple_dedicated_for_a_hindu_section and coverage_under_amended_definition_admitted

predicates.temple_entry_scope_case: The proceeding concerns whether a temple falls within a law governing entry into Hindu public temples.
predicates.private_status_not_pleaded: The party claiming that the temple is private did not plead that claim.
predicates.temple_dedicated_for_a_hindu_section: The temple was dedicated for the benefit of a section of the Hindu community.
predicates.coverage_under_amended_definition_admitt: The party challenging coverage admitted that the temple came within the applicable amended definition.

issues.definition: When a temple-entry proceeding concerns a temple dedicated for the benefit of a Hindu section, and private status was not pleaded while coverage under the applicable definition was admitted, the temple falls within the public-entry law.

issues.legal_issue: A temple originally dedicated for the benefit of a particular religious community remains denominational even if members of other communities are allowed to worship there.
material_facts: The temple was founded for the benefit of the Gowda Saraswath Brahmin community, whose members had brought their idols with them and established the temple after settling in the area.
The community followed the head of a religious mutt, who performed important ceremonies and had authority in temple matters.
The evidence showed that people outside the community were excluded from certain religious ceremonies, although members of other communities were also admitted to worship at other times.
issues.conclusion: The temple was a denominational temple founded for the benefit of the Gowda Saraswath Brahmin community. The admission of members of other communities did not enlarge the original dedication to benefit the public generally.
issues.legal_principle: The nature and extent of a temple’s dedication are determined from the endowment deed, if available, or other legally admissible evidence; long and uninterrupted use may be cogent evidence of the dedication. But where dedication to a particular community is proved, allowing others to worship does not establish that the dedication was also for their benefit. The Court relied on Babu Bhagwan Din v. Gir Har Saroop, (1939) L.R. 67 I.A. 1.

predicates.denominational_status_case: The proceeding requires the court to determine whether a temple is denominational.
predicates.original_dedication_for_a_particular_rel: The temple was originally founded for the benefit of a particular religious community.
predicates.other_communities_later_allowed_to_worsh: Members of other communities were later allowed to worship at the temple.

issues.definition: In a proceeding about denominational status, a proven original dedication to a particular religious community remains determinative even if other communities are later allowed to worship.

issues.legal_issue: Rules determining who may enter a temple for worship and how worship is conducted are matters of religion protected by the right of a religious denomination to manage its religious affairs.
material_facts: The temple was founded for the benefit of a religious denomination.

The evidence and the relevant ceremonial practices showed that members of the denomination alone could participate in certain ceremonies, while other worshippers were subject to rules about access and participation.
issues.conclusion: Temple-entry and worship practices prescribed by the ceremonial law are matters of religion. If considered solely under Article 26(b), the denominational right would include excluding persons not entitled to participate in worship under the institution’s tenets; that right remains subject to the separate public-entry protection considered by the Court.
issues.legal_principle: In The Commissioner, Hindu Religious Endowments, Madras v. Sri Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar of Sri Shirur Mutt, (1954) S.C.R. 1005, the Court held that matters of religion include practices regarded by the community as part of its religion. The Court also relied on Gopala Muppanar v. Subramania Aiyar, (1914) 27 M.L.J. 253, concerning ceremonial rules about worship and access, and Sankaralinga Nadan v. Raja Rajeswara Dorai, (1908) L.R. 35 I.A. 176, concerning the trustee’s duty to follow the temple’s Agamas and custom. Article 26(b) protects management of religious affairs, subject to the harmonious operation of Article 25(2)(b).

predicates.denominational_religious_rights_case: The proceeding concerns a denomination’s asserted right to manage a temple’s religious affairs.
predicates.ceremonial_rules_govern_access_or_partic: Ceremonial rules of the institution determine who may enter, participate in worship, or take part in particular services.

issues.definition: When a denomination’s religious-management rights are at issue and its ceremonial rules govern access or participation, those access and worship practices are religious matters.

issues.legal_issue: The public right to enter Hindu religious institutions of a public character under a valid temple-entry law controls a denomination’s claim to exclude the public from worship altogether.
material_facts: The temple was a public institution dedicated for the benefit of a section of the Hindu public, although it was denominational.
The challenged provision entitled members of excluded classes to enter Hindu temples and offer worship.
The denomination claimed a right to exclude all persons outside its community from worship.
issues.conclusion: Denominational temples are included among religious institutions of a public character. Article 25(2)(b) controls Article 26(b) to the extent necessary to secure the public’s right of entry for worship, so the provision opening the temple to all classes and sections of Hindus was valid.
issues.legal_principle: Article 25(2)(b) extends to religious institutions of a public character, including institutions founded for the benefit of a section of the public and denominational temples. Article 25(2) addresses community rights and controls both Article 25(1) and Article 26(b) on temple entry. The two provisions must be harmoniously construed: the public-entry right prevails against total exclusion, while denominational religious rights remain effective where they can be accommodated without making the public right nugatory. Section 3 of the Madras Temple Entry Authorisation Act, 1947, was protected by Article 25(2)(b).

rule.if: constitutional_public_entry_case and temple_is_public_institution and law_opens_temple_to_all_hindu_classes and denomination_claims_total_exclusion

predicates.constitutional_public_entry_case: The proceeding concerns a claimed constitutional right of public entry to a Hindu temple.
predicates.temple_is_public_institution: The temple is a public religious institution, including one founded for the benefit of a section of the public.
predicates.law_opens_temple_to_all_hindu_classes: A law provides that all classes and sections of Hindus may enter the temple for worship.
predicates.denomination_claims_total_exclusion: The denomination claims the right to exclude the public from worship in the temple altogether.

issues.definition: In a constitutional public-entry proceeding, a law opening a public temple to all Hindu classes prevails over a denomination’s claim to exclude the public altogether.

issues.legal_issue: A denomination may reserve strictly denominational ceremonies from public participation when the public retains a substantial opportunity to worship at other times.
material_facts: The temple’s members claimed that only members of their denomination could participate in certain ceremonies and on special occasions.
Uncontradicted evidence established the denomination’s exclusive participation in those ceremonies, and the finding was not challenged.
Other occasions for public worship remained numerous and substantial.
The High Court’s decree preserved the denomination’s exclusion during the specified ceremonies and occasions.
issues.conclusion: The limited exclusions were protected by Article 26(b) and were consistent with Article 25(2)(b), because they concerned strictly denominational services and left the public with a substantial right of worship. The High Court’s decree struck a proper balance and was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: The public-entry right is a right to enter for worship, but it is not absolute or unlimited. Article 25(2)(b) must be harmonized with Article 26(b). Denominational restrictions may be recognized where they are strictly denominational and leave the public with a substantial, rather than merely nominal, opportunity to worship; if the restrictions substantially reduce the public right, the denominational claim must yield.

predicates.constitutional_public_entry_case: The proceeding concerns the balance between public temple-entry rights and denominational religious rights.
predicates.exclusion_limited_to_denominational_serv: The claimed exclusion applies only to particular services or occasions rather than to public worship generally.
predicates.evidence_supports_exclusive_participatio: Evidence establishes that participation in those services or occasions is reserved to the denomination.
predicates.public_retains_substantial_worship_oppor: The public retains numerous or otherwise substantial opportunities to worship at the temple.

issues.definition: When exclusion is confined to evidenced denominational services and the public retains substantial opportunities to worship, the limited exclusion is valid.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in seeking appellate review may be condoned when resolving the appeal on its merits is just because the litigation affects the rights of the public and final resolution is appropriate.
material_facts: The State’s application for leave to appeal was substantially out of time.
The State had not appealed earlier and had opposed the other party’s request for leave, but the outcome of the litigation affected members of the public.
The Court considered it just to determine the controversy on its merits so that it could be finally settled.
issues.conclusion: The Court condoned the delay and heard the application on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: Although acquiescing in a judgment and allowing the appeal period to lapse ordinarily does not justify condonation merely because the party later changes its mind, the Court may condone delay where the litigation affects public rights and a decision on the merits is just to settle the controversy finally.

predicates.late_appellate_application: A party makes an appellate application after the applicable time for filing has expired.
predicates.application_affects_public_rights: The outcome of the appellate proceeding affects rights of members of the public.
predicates.merits_review_needed_for_final_resolutio: Determining the merits is considered just to settle the controversy finally.

issues.definition: When a late appellate application affects public rights and merits review is needed for final resolution, the delay is condoned.
